Queenston Heights: The southern terminus of the Bruce Trail. The cairn marking the start sits at the edge of the parking lot below Brock's Monument, an 1850s column topped by a 16-foot statue of Sir Isaac Brock, who was killed in the 1812 Battle of Queenston Heights.
General Brock Side Trail: An out-and-back of about 6 km each way on this blue-blazed side trail. We could not find a published description of its terrain or features.
Road walking: The General Brock Side Trail follows road shoulders in six separate stretches on this route. Keep Zappy on a short leash and close to you on those sections.
Dogs: Leashed dogs are welcome on the Bruce Trail and its side trails. The park itself has picnic pavilions, a splash pad and monuments, so expect other visitors near the start.

subtitle: Woodend Conservation Area
expect: Parking: Woodend Conservation Area is entered from Taylor Rd, 140 m north of Warner Rd. Parking and entry are free, but the lot is limited, so arrive early on weekends.

Margaret Kalogeropoulos Side Trail: This blue-blazed side trail starts with a short road-shoulder stretch; keep Zappy close. It pairs with the main trail for a short loop through shaded hardwood forest with Carolinian trees such as black cherry and sugar maple.

Main Bruce Trail: Runs along the escarpment edge past rock outcrops and a stacked-stone wall. The ground is uneven but the walking is easy. Blazes aren't always on trees, so watch the ground too. Highway noise carries at times.

Wetland Ridge & Niagara College Side Trails: These lead to Niagara College's campus, where old sewage lagoons have become a 7-hectare wetland with interpretive signs. The route passes a First Nations, Métis and Inuit Garden and the college Teaching Winery, which has the area's only washroom.
Dogs: Leashed dogs are welcome on the Bruce Trail. No park-specific dog rules were found.

Main Bruce Trail: Near here the main trail makes its first real drop down the escarpment, with steps and a switchback or two. It can be muddy near the old quarry.

expect: Parking: Enter from Pelham Rd. Short Hills has three parking lots and few other facilities. There are toilets at the Pelham Rd lot. The park opens at sunrise and closes at dusk.

Black Walnut Side Trail: A short out-and-back on a blue-blazed natural-surface side trail that crosses a low-lying area. The park's Black Walnut Trail runs alongside part of the Bruce Trail and is rated for steep hills and uneven ground. It is shared with cyclists and horse riders.

Closures and wet weather: Storm and flood damage has closed parts of several park trails, including a section of the Black Walnut Trail. The park asks visitors to stay off trails when they are wet. Check current alerts before you go.
Dogs: Ontario Parks requires dogs on a leash no longer than 2 m (6 ft). Waste bags and bins are at the park entrances.

Main Bruce Trail, road sections: Around Glendale the main trail goes through urban St. Catharines. It uses road shoulders and paved paths, and the route crosses the canal on a bridge. Keep Zappy close on these stretches.

Main Bruce Trail, Old Welland Canal: Off-road, the main trail follows the Third Welland Canal (1887-1931) past its abandoned locks. The lock walls are high with a long drop, so keep away from the edges.
Bert Lowe Side Trail: An out-and-back on this blue-blazed side trail, which starts from a road section of the main trail. We could not find a published description of its terrain or features.
Cautions: Nearby on the main trail, signs mark property with sewage lagoons; stay on the marked route. In fall, bird-scaring devices make loud shotgun-like booms that may startle a dog.
Dogs: Leashed dogs are welcome on the Bruce Trail and its side trails.

The Twelve Side Trail: This blue-blazed side trail follows Twelve Mile Creek through St. Catharines. It changes from singletrack to a wide groomed or gravel path, open in some places and wooded in others. There are no steep sections. You'll pass under overpasses and may see deer at the creek.
The Twelve Side Trail-01: A connected branch of the same side trail. A pedestrian bridge north of Glendale crosses the creek and links trails on both banks.
Road walking: Two stretches of the Twelve Side Trail follow a road shoulder on this route. Keep Zappy close.
Dogs: Leashed dogs are welcome on the Bruce Trail and its side trails.

subtitle: Beamer Memorial Conservation Area, Grimsby
expect: Parking: Start from the Grimsby Lions Community Pool lot, entering at 1 Elm St at the south end of Coronation Park.

Forty Mile Creek Side Trail: In April 2026 this side trail was extended to 1.5 km over the former main Trail route, so it now runs up the wooded Forty Mile Creek valley to the corner of Mountain Street and Ridge Road East.

Road walking: The BTC notice says the main Trail now follows Mountain Street to Ridge Road West, so expect road-shoulder walking on this stretch. Ridge Road is busy; keep Zappy close and stay off the roadway.

Beamers Falls: The former Beamers Falls Side Trail is now main Trail from the Ridge Road West parking area, so look for white blazes rather than blue. Upper Beamer Falls is about 6 m high; the best view is from beside Ridge Road.

Grimsby Point Side Trail: A short spur to escarpment-top lookouts at Beamer Memorial Conservation Area, a well-known spring hawk-watch site. The central observation deck closes from February 28 to May 15 for bird migration; the other lookouts stay open. Stay back from the cliff edges.

Staircase closure: A damaged staircase in the conservation area was closed in April 2026 and the Trail was rerouted around it; a GVTA hike in July 2026 still described it as closed. A short leftover piece of the old route, reached from Gibson Street, is not part of the Bruce Trail. Follow the current blazes.
Cautions: The scramble up the creek to Lower Beamer Falls is not an official trail and has loose, slippery rocks. Stay on the blazed route.

subtitle: Mountainview Conservation Area, Beamsville
expect: Parking: Enter the Mountainview Conservation Area lot from Mountainview Rd. The NPCA lists the area as open year-round, sunrise to sunset, for passive use (hiking and birdwatching) only, with no facilities such as washrooms.

Mountainview Conservation Area: About 25 hectares of Carolinian forest on the Niagara Escarpment, with exposed dolostone, many bedrock fractures and eroded talus slopes. Watch your footing and keep Zappy away from cracks in the rock.

Lookouts: The NPCA notes several Bruce Trail lookout points here with views over the Iroquois plain to Lake Ontario. Trails climb gently through hardwood forest before opening onto the escarpment edge; stay back from drop-offs.

Side trails: A short loop through the Beamsville Bench, Angel and Mountainview side trails. Specific descriptions of these three side trails were not found, so expect the same mix of forest path and rocky escarpment terrain as the rest of the area.

subtitle: Louth Conservation Area
expect: Parking: Louth Conservation Area is entered from Staff Ave, 500 m north of Pelham Rd (Regional Rd 69). Signage is sparse. There are no washrooms. The area is open year-round from sunrise to sunset; NPCA gives no fee details (905-788-3135).
Staff Avenue Side Trail: A well-defined path from the lot into the woods that meets the main trail. Horses use this trail, so watch for them.

Main Bruce Trail & Louth Falls: Escarpment forest above the Sixteen Mile Creek valley, with old rock formations and songbirds. Louth Falls is near the Louth Side Trail junction. The gorge has no easy way down, so enjoy the view from above.
Louth & Midway Side Trails: Short side trails off the main trail; the Louth Side Trail does not lead to the falls. No terrain details were found.

Dogs & hemlocks: NPCA asks you to stay on trails and keep dogs leashed. This helps limit the spread of hemlock woolly adelgid, an invasive pest found nearby. Clean boots and gear, and don't take branches or twigs.

expect: Parking: Roadside on Leslie Dr west of New Mountain Rd, just north of the railway bridge. The Hamilton Conservation Authority (HCA) lot at the Punch Bowl itself charges $8.50 a day (pay at the machine); this route starts from the free roadside spot instead.
Devil's Punch Bowl Side Trail: HCA says the side trail runs down a section of Ridge Rd before joining the main Trail, so keep Zappy close and watch for traffic there.

The Punch Bowl: A 33.8 m ribbon falls (upper) and a 5.5 m lower falls in a deep gorge. Lookouts show bands of red Queenston shale, grey shale and limestone, with views over Stoney Creek and Hamilton Harbour. A lit steel cross stands beside the gorge.

Cautions: HCA warns that loose rock falls often and without warning. Stay behind the fences; going to the bottom of the falls is prohibited. Below the escarpment the Bruce Trail is the only permitted route, and you can see the lower falls safely from it. Keep well back from the rim.

Main Trail and short side trails: The main Trail links the New Mountain Road and Oakridge Drive side trails to the Punch Bowl. A club hike description mentions escarpment-edge walking with some hills and uneven footing. No details were found for the two short side trails.

subtitle: Borer's Falls / Rock Chapel
expect: Parking: The Borer's Dog Park lot on York Rd just south of Valley Rd, described by a trip report as free. Tourism Hamilton suggests arriving early or on weekdays and not parking on the roadside if lots are full.

Ray Lowes Side Trail: Named for Ray Lowes, who first proposed a continuous escarpment trail in 1959. Expect hard-packed dirt with occasional roots and rocks, and some climbing; one writer calls the walk from the dog park toward the falls "an uphill battle." This is a short out-and-back.

Along the way: A trip report on this side trail mentions the railway bridge over York Rd (trains are frequent), a cut-stone culvert just west of York Rd, and the 1860 Rasberry farmhouse with a leaning stone silo.

Borer's Falls nearby: The 15 m curtain falls (also called Rock Chapel Falls) is about 30-40 minutes' walk from the dog park, beyond this route. Flow is seasonal and best after rain or in early spring.

Cautions: Do not cross the active CN rail tracks. Stay on marked trails (the area has rare plants), keep back from slopes and edges, and keep Zappy close. Watch for poison ivy in summer and slippery footing in winter.

Main Bruce Trail: Runs beside the Chedoke Radial Trail, a former railway line (1908-1931). A 2015 trip report describes a long set of steps up to a Lower Chedoke Falls lookout, metal steps near the Chedoke golf club, and woods and open meadows through Iroquoia Heights Conservation Area. Expect stairs.
Iroquoia Heights Side Trail: Mapped as nearly level (about 1% average grade), running from near Scenic Dr and forming a loop with the main trail through Iroquoia Heights Conservation Area.

Scenic Falls: Near the west end of the Chedoke Radial Trail by Scenic Dr, a roughly 18 m falls in a small gorge. It is best after heavy rain, and trees limit the view. Details of the Scenic Woods Side Trail itself were not found.
Robert MacLaren and Hillcrest Ave side trails: Short connectors; no further details were found.
Length: At 12.9 km this is a long day; plan water and rest stops for Zappy.

subtitle: Spencer Gorge (Tew Falls & Dundas Peak)
expect: Parking: Off-road at the lookout on Sydenham Rd. HCA's Spencer Gorge lots need a reservation ($11 per vehicle plus $5.50 per passenger and a $10 booking fee); this route starts outside the gorge instead.
Road walking: The Sydenham Lookout Side Trail and two stretches of the main trail follow road shoulders. Keep Zappy close.

Tews Falls Side Trail: Leads to Tew Falls, where Logie's Creek drops 41 m into the gorge. There are two viewing platforms (the upper one by stairs), then an uphill trail to Dundas Peak with views of Hamilton Harbour, Dundas and Cootes Paradise.
Glen Ferguson Side Trail: About 1 km of moderate inclines and uneven ground. It branches off the Tews Falls trail and rejoins it near Dundas Peak, so the route weaves between the two.
Cautions and dogs: HCA requires pets on leash and picked up after. Keep at least a body length back from gorge and escarpment edges, stay on marked trails, and do not go to the bottom of the falls.
Main Bruce Trail: Escarpment-edge walking over the Dundas Valley, with roots, rocks and possible mud after rain.

expect: Parking: Lot beside Mill St at the Smokey Hollow Side Trail, right by the falls (a trip report describes it as free).

Great Falls: About 10 m high on Grindstone Creek, with an overhanging dolostone cap and remains of an old mill dam and stone abutments. The Smokey Hollow Side Trail leads to a viewing platform above the crest. The creek banks get slippery and icy; stay back from the edge.

Main Bruce Trail: Steps and switchbacks on the Grindstone Creek valley slopes near the falls, and several short road-shoulder stretches (including Flanders Dr); keep Zappy close. A lookout past King Rd gives views of Burlington and Lake Ontario.

Norman Pearson and McNally side trails: The Norman Pearson Side Trail (blue-blazed) runs from level ground on the main trail to Waterdown Rd, including a road stretch. It connects to the McNally Side Trail, which crosses BTC-owned land with a reported overlook of Burlington Bay and tall trees along the escarpment edge.
Eric Best and King side trails: No specific descriptions were found. Around King Rd the main trail passes through Conservation Halton's Waterdown Woods: a grassy field and mature hardwoods.
Private land: Much of the trail here crosses private property by landowner permission. Stay on the marked trail.

Main Bruce Trail: A 2015 trip report describes the trail skirting Kerncliff Park and dropping into a wooded valley, then climbing back out. North toward King Rd, a lookout gives views of Burlington and Lake Ontario.

subtitle: Rattlesnake Point & Crawford Lake
expect: Parking: Rattlesnake Point Conservation Area, entered from Appleby Line 1 km north of Derry Rd. Gate fees apply and a reservation system is in effect; booking online also saves on the gate fee. Open 8:30 a.m. to 7 p.m. The lower lot closes in winter and the upper lot is small; do not park on nearby roads.

Rattlesnake Point Side Trail: Inside the conservation area along the escarpment cliffs. Buffalo Crag Lookout has one of the best views on the escarpment, and turkey vultures often soar overhead. The cliffs are used for rock climbing, so keep Zappy close near edges.
Leech Porter Side Trail: Crosses Nassagaweya Canyon on a 150 m boardwalk over Limestone Creek. Expect a gradual descent into forest and a steady climb up the canyon wall.

Crawford Lake Side Trail: Reaches Crawford Lake Conservation Area, with its boardwalk around a meromictic lake and a reconstructed 15th-century longhouse village. Main trails there include steep, rocky slopes.
Dogs: Conservation Halton requires leashes no longer than 2 m. Dogs may not swim in Crawford Lake.
Length: At 12.6 km this is a full day; bring plenty of water for you and Zappy.

subtitle: Hilton Falls Conservation Area
expect: Parking: Enter from Campbellville Rd. A reservation system is in effect; Conservation Halton recommends booking online, which secures a spot and can lower the gate fee. Listed park hours are 8:30 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Philip Gosling Side Trail: A short link from the main lot to the Bruce Trail. A trip report notes the reservoir stays hidden behind a ridge along this stretch.

Hilton Falls Side Trail: Leads to the falls, which flow in every season. Stone remains of three 19th-century sawmills sit at the brow, and a small viewing platform is reached by stairs. The rocks below are slippery; keep Zappy back from wet rock.
Main trail and the Gap: The Bruce Trail crosses “The Gap,” an open-pit quarry cut in 1962, on a footbridge with views over the active quarry, farmland and, on clear days, distant skylines.
Restoration Side Trail: A brief spur looking over a closed section of the quarry that is being restored to natural land.
Road walking: Two stretches of the main trail follow a road shoulder; keep Zappy close and walk single file facing traffic.
Shared trails: The park also has mountain-bike single-track, and horses are allowed on its red, purple and yellow trails (not on the Bruce Trail). Watch for bikes and horses where trails meet.

expect: Parking: Lot at 10200 Sixth Line Nassagaweya, giving access to the Hilton Falls Side Trail. This is an out-and-back walk on the blue-blazed side trail, so you retrace your steps to the car.

Wet ground: A trip report from a Sixth Line start notes the dolomite bedrock here holds water in pools near the surface, and many trees fall in the wet conditions. Expect soggy patches and blowdowns, especially in spring.

Along the way: The same report mentions a glacial pothole beside the blue trail, an old stone fence through the forest, and a sluice gate controlling the wetlands. It put the scenic route to the falls at about 6 km from Sixth Line.

Hilton Falls: The falls flow in every season, with stone remains of 19th-century sawmills at the brow and a small stair-access viewing platform. Rocks below the falls are slippery; keep Zappy back from wet rock.
Busy area: Inside Hilton Falls Conservation Area you may meet mountain bikers and, on some park trails, horses.

subtitle: Silver Creek, Halton Hills
expect: Parking: Small roadside parking on Sixth Line where the main Trail exits the forest. The BTC lists two new spots on Sixth Line (about 5 and 3 cars); cars must be completely off the pavement to be legally parked. Silver Creek parking can fill on weekends from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and there are no washrooms.

New trails: The Sixth Line (480 m) and Beeney Creek (820 m) side trails are part of the July 2026 Silver Creek reconfiguration, which moved the main Trail onto a more natural route and took about 1.2 km of trail off Sixth Line. No published descriptions of these two side trails were found yet.

Terrain: Credit Valley Conservation describes Silver Creek trails as having steep slopes, rocks and roots, and rates the Bruce Trail here strenuous, with long steep climbs and wooden bridges. Expect some of that even on this short loop.

Older maps: After the July 2026 Silver Creek reconfiguration, the Duff Pit, Trafalgar and Great Esker side trails no longer appear under those names; parts became main Trail or were renamed. Follow the current blazes and the guide's directions.

expect: Parking: Bruce Trail lot on 22 Sideroad just west of Fourth Line. A trip report notes the trail meets the road at a blind curve with no shoulders, so take care stepping out of the trees.

Canada Goose Side Trail: Runs about 3 km along an escarpment ridge roughly parallel to Fourth Line. Footing is described as challenging: rocks, wet spots, stumps and roots. It passes the old silo and stone barn foundations of a homestead and skirts a limestone quarry.
Black Creek Side Trail: Credit Valley Conservation rates it difficult, following the creek through several forest types with steep grades in places; CVC lists dog walking on this trail.

Main trail and stiles: The main trail crosses private land and uses stiles over fences; be ready to help Zappy over. Near Limehouse the main trail passes rock fissures and ladders at the Hole in the Wall, which CVC calls unsuitable for pets.
Road walking: A stretch of the main trail and the final stretch of the Canada Goose Side Trail follow a road shoulder; keep Zappy close and walk single file facing traffic.
Short connectors: No descriptions were found for the Charles Hildebrandt or Brown Benton side trails.

subtitle: Limehouse Conservation Area
expect: Parking: At the baseball diamonds, reached from Fifth Line just southeast of Limehouse village. Entry is free; there are no washrooms.

Main trail through Limehouse: Credit Valley Conservation rates it difficult, with stone, soil, steps, a ladder and steep grades. It passes rock fissures and the Hole in the Wall, where a ladder leads down into cracks in the escarpment. CVC says this trail is not suitable for pets because of the terrain, so plan how you will handle Zappy here.
History: Watch for a restored 1870s lime kiln, a restored powder house once used to store blasting powder, old mill remains near the Black Creek bridge, and a lookout over the railway tracks.
Road walking: Two short stretches of the main trail follow a road shoulder (a trip report names Kirkpatrick Lane and Fifth Line near Limehouse); keep Zappy close and walk single file facing traffic.
Side trails: No descriptions were found for the Ridge or Todd Bardes Meadowland side trails; follow the blue blazes.

Cheltenham Badlands: The Toronto Section ends near these Queenston Shale badlands, now viewed from a boardwalk. Visitors leaving the trail worsened the erosion, so stay on the path if you visit.

subtitle: Scotsdale Farm and Silver Creek
expect: Parking: Scotsdale Farm, an Ontario Heritage Trust property; enter from Trafalgar Rd, 1.7 km northwest of Highway 7. Credit Valley Conservation notes there are no washrooms in the Silver Creek area and parking fills on weekends from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Bennett Heritage Trail: Starts at Scotsdale Farm and passes a pond with a weeping willow, then crosses Snow's Creek and Owl Creek. CVC rates it difficult.

Maureen Smith and Silver Creek side trails: CVC rates both difficult. Maureen Smith has steep sections with rocks and boulders; the short Silver Creek Side Trail links it to the main Trail and crosses streams. The Maureen Smith Side Trail was lengthened in the July 2026 reconfiguration.
Main Trail: Reworked in July 2026 onto a more natural route. CVC rates the Bruce Trail here strenuous, with escarpment views, wooden bridges and long steep climbs.
North Rim and Reservoir side trails: The North Rim Side Trail (opened 2024) crosses an open, regenerating former quarry site. No description of the Reservoir Side Trail was found.
Snows Creek Side Trail: Rebuilt as a 3.6 km side trail in July 2026 and leads back toward Scotsdale Farm. No published description of its terrain was found.

Older maps: After the July 2026 Silver Creek reconfiguration, the Duff Pit, Trafalgar and Great Esker side trails no longer appear under those names; parts became main Trail or were renamed. Follow the current blazes and the guide's directions.

expect: Parking: Roadside on Prince Street (20th Sideroad) across from the cemetery. This is an out-and-back walk, so you retrace your steps to the car.

Credit Valley Footpath: A blue-blazed side trail that follows part of the Credit River. A hiking club describes roots, rocks, some river crossings, and ground that is very hilly and rugged in spots; it recommends waterproof boots, poles and insect repellent.
Steps: A trip report mentions steps on the descent between the main trail and the footpath near Tenth Line.
History: The whole footpath runs almost 10 km and leads to the 1837 Barber Paper Mills in Georgetown and, downstream, the site of an early Barber dynamo. These may lie beyond today's turnaround.

expect: Parking: Roadside on Tenth Line, 2.2 km southeast of 32 Sideroad. Silver Creek parking is roadside only and can fill on weekends from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Entry is free; no washrooms.
Walking Fern Side Trail: Follows the valley bottom and is rated difficult. Look for walking fern and other unusual plants; CVC also notes an escarpment lookout.
Main trail: CVC calls the Bruce Trail here strenuous, with long steep climbs, rocks, boulders, roots, fallen trees and narrow sections. Streams are crossed on wooden bridges.
Roberts Side Trail: Rated moderate, through mature woods with a boardwalk past a pond that protects Jefferson salamander habitat.

Irwin Quarry Side Trail: Rated difficult. It visits one of about 50 small quarries along the escarpment, worked because the soil over the limestone was so thin; the exposed limestone has since been replanted.
Dogs: CVC lists dog walking on several Silver Creek trails.

route: Devils Pulpit Side Trail > Trimble Side Trail > Crow's Nest Side Trail > Trimble Side Trail > Devils Pulpit Side Trail > Ring Kiln Side Trail > Devils Pulpit Side Trail
subtitle: Devil's Pulpit & Forks of the Credit (Belfountain)
expect: Parking: roadside on the east side of Creditview Rd, just north of Grange Sideroad. Trip reports note that parking at this trailhead is limited, so arrive early.

Devil's Pulpit Side Trail: the hard part of the day: steep rock faces and stairs one hiking club calls 'treacherous', plus boulders to scramble over (about 150 m down and back up). Wear boots; poles help. Since 2023, Dominion Street construction has moved part of the main Trail onto this side trail, so you may see white blazes.
Road walking: several stretches of the Devil's Pulpit and Trimble side trails follow road shoulders. Keep the dog close and on a short leash.

Trimble Side Trail: named for founding members Roy and Eleanor Trimble. It runs beside the Credit River toward Belfountain, with a view of the curved Credit Valley Railway trestle. Stonecutter's Dam, an old masonry dam, is posted; stay off it.

Crow's Nest Side Trail: a 1 km loop that starts on a boardwalk, then follows an old quarry road past test pits from the 1880s Crow's Nest Quarry, source of sandstone for the Ontario Legislature. A fence line runs above a steep drop to Forks of the Credit Rd; keep the dog away from the edge.

Ring Kiln Side Trail: a short spur to the ruins of a Hoffman lime kiln built around 1896 that ran for only about three years. The collapsed chimney left a 6 m-deep hole, now covered by a steel grate; don't climb on the ruins.
Dogs: allowed on leash. On the steep rock and stairs, a short leash makes it easier to keep your footing.

parking_details: Forks of the Credit Parking Area: Enter from McLaren Rd (1.9 km south of Peel Rd 24). From the lot, take either the Meadow Trail or the Trans Canada Trail to the main Trail.
trails: Mill Pond Side Trail (1.6 km); Cataract Side Trail (1.1 km)
route: Main Trail > Mill Pond Side Trail > Main Trail > Cataract Side Trail > Main Trail
subtitle: Forks of the Credit Provincial Park
expect: Parking: the Ontario Parks lot off McLaren Rd has limited space, and an advance daily vehicle permit is required (no entry without one). Permits open at 7 am five days ahead, as 4-hour slots or a full day, at reservations.ontarioparks.com or 1-888-668-7275. Roadside parking on nearby roads can be ticketed or towed.
Getting to the main Trail: the park notes the Meadow Trail connection has been closed for infrastructure damage. If it's still signed closed, use the Trans Canada Trail from the lot.
Mill Pond Side Trail: named for the reservoir that powered a grist mill over the falls; John Deagle later used the site to generate electricity. Expect metal stairs on this trail.

Cataract Side Trail: leads to a lookout over Cataract Falls (about 13-14 m high and 9 m wide) and follows the Credit River. The stone foundations of the Cataract Electric Company (1899-1947) sit at the crest of the falls. View the ruins from the trail.
Main Bruce Trail: white blazes through the park on the Niagara Escarpment. Construction at the Forks of the Credit has caused temporary reroutes nearby, so follow current blazes and signs.
Dogs: Ontario Parks rules: leash no longer than 2 m, and pick up after your dog. Ticks are common here; check yourself and the dog afterwards.

subtitle: Song Bird Nature Reserve & Meltwater Moraine
expect: Parking: roadside on the west side of Airport Road, across from Finnerty Sideroad. Airport Road is busy, so load the dog on the side away from traffic.

Road walking: since the main Trail moved off Airport Road in 2025, the Songbird Side Trail is no longer connected to it, and you walk a stretch of road shoulder to reach it. Several shorter main-Trail stretches also follow road shoulders. Keep the dog close.

Songbird Side Trail: passes through mature sugar maple forest, hedgerows and thickets, and old farm meadow now in native grasses. It's an eBird hotspot; listen for Indigo Bunting, Brown Thrasher, Bobolink and Eastern Meadowlark. Volunteers hauled out two bins of scrap metal in 2012, the year the trail was blazed.

Meltwater Side Trail: A 420 m side trail opened in July 2025 in the Meltwater Moraine protected natural area, which the BTC secured that year. With the main Trail it makes a 1.3 km loop through the northeastern part of the property; this route uses it twice.

Dogs: allowed on leash, but not on the Paris Moraine Side Trail, which branches off this part of the main Trail: the BTC made it a no-dog zone (between Escarpment Sideroad and the main Trail), so this plan leaves it out. Keep Zappy on the trail in the meadows, where ground-nesting birds like Bobolink live.

expect: Parking: the Bruce Trail lot on the 7th Line just east of Airport Rd, built in 2002 for hikers. The Town of Mono lists room for about 15 cars. A short access trail (0.2 km, partly along the road) links it to the main Trail.

Glen Haffy Side Trail: blue blazes; with the main Trail it makes a loop. It passes farm fences, a pine plantation planted to hold back sand dunes left after early logging, a wooden stile, and a small bridge over the Humber River under hemlocks. Then a steep climb onto a ridge with farmland views and mature hardwoods.
Highway 9 crossing: the side trail's write-up warns that traffic here is fast. Cross carefully with the dog on a short leash.
Spring: look for bloodroot, trillium, hepatica, trout lily and Dutchman's breeches in the woods.
Winter: the club asks hikers to follow alternate-route signs near the 7th Line lot and stay off cross-country ski trails.
Dogs: allowed on leash throughout.

Harmony Side Trail: a short link you'll pass several times. It was kept as a loop connector when the main Trail was rerouted through the Taoist Tai Chi Society property in the late 1980s.

Darcy's Side Trail: the only side trail on the whole Bruce Trail named after a dog: Darcy, a Jack Russell terrier who ran in these woods for 19 years. The land is now a Bruce Trail Conservancy protected area called Tall Timbers. A fitting one for Zappy.
Hockleycrest Side Trail: crosses the 'Moule Easement', land donated by Sally Cohen and Dave Moule. The short Hockleycrest Shortcut links it back to the main Trail.
Hockley Hollow Side Trail: a short spur to an overnight rest area.
Terrain: we didn't find detailed terrain notes for these trails. Expect woodland walking with the hills typical of the Hockley area.
Dogs: allowed on leash. The club's Darcy's Side Trail story asks hikers to keep dogs leashed and pack out their waste.

expect: Parking: Bruce Trail parking lot on 2nd Line EHS at the start of the Splitrock Side Trail; it is plowed in winter. The nature reserve's address is listed as 755437 2nd Line EHS, Mono.

Splitrock Side Trail: Starts across farmland, then enters forest that follows a long split in the rock and finishes in cedar woods near the road. Wildflowers, a cave and a spring are noted along the way. A local organizer describes the reserve as having "cliffs, fantastic views, caves, and rock cut outs."
Caution at the split: Where the crack in the rock is narrow it is also very deep. Keep Zappy on a short leash and stay on the trail near the edges.
Narrows Side Trail: A short drop of about 150 m down into the narrows, with small caverns and rock walls. You come back up the same way.
Ralph Tremills Side Trail: A 1 km side trail off the Splitrock Side Trail. No description of it was found.

subtitle: Hockley Heights & Mono forest tracts
expect: Parking: the Bruce Trail lot on the east side of 5th Line EHS, just south of Hockley Rd.

Hockley Heights Side Trail: the club calls it strenuous, with steep hills and valleys. It runs through pine and maple forest planted by Mono Township from 1926, partly by local Boys and Girls' Forestry Clubs. At the top is the 100-acre Anderson Tract, marked by a Town of Mono sign.
Road walking: parts of the Hockley Heights Side Trail follow road shoulders. Keep the dog close.

Hemlock Ridge Side Trail: follows a steep-sided ridge built from glacial meltwater sediment, with eastern hemlocks (some of this species live over 500 years). The club notes the steep sides make a good workout.
Glacier Valley Side Trail: a 580 m path through a forested valley. Near its eastern end with the main Trail is a marked sugar maple that ecologists date to before Confederation (1867).
Dogs: allowed on leash throughout. Bring plenty of water for both of you on the hills.

subtitle: Riverside Woods & Hockley Valley nature reserves
expect: Parking: the Bruce Trail lot on the east side of 1st Line EHS. The Upland Side Trail branches off the Goodyear Memorial Side Trail just east of the lot.

Goodyear Memorial and Upland side trails (Riverside Woods Nature Reserve): a former Scout camp the Bruce Trail Conservancy bought in 2023. Pine stands and meadows being restored to native grassland. The Upland trail is flat, with a bench at a view north and east. Stay away from the old camp buildings, which are unsafe.

Toward the Nottawasaga River: the Goodyear Memorial Side Trail drops into the river valley and climbs back out, the day's main ups and downs. The short Rushing River Side Trail (about 200 m) leads down to the river.
Road walking: the white-blazed main Bruce Trail follows a road shoulder for a stretch, walked both ways. Keep the dog close.

Tom East Side Trail (Hockley Valley Provincial Nature Reserve): 2.5 km through rolling woodland, making a loop with the main Trail. It's named for Tom East, who led the first Bruce Trail guidebook (1965). The reserve has no visitor facilities.

History: Goodyear bought the land in 1946 as a memorial to employees who died in the Second World War, and it was a Scout camp until 2016. James Dodds' 1857 stone house is on private land; view it from the trail only.
Dogs: allowed on leash throughout. Check for ticks after the meadows.

expect: Parking: the lot on the east side of 3rd Line EHS. A short trail on the west side of the road leads to the Glen Cross Side Trail. There's no fee.

Glen Cross and Isabel East side trails: with the Tom East Side Trail, these make up the Bruce Trail 'Jeju Olle' Friendship Trail, twinned with a route on Korea's Jeju Island. Isabel East, a long-time club volunteer and president, was Tom East's wife. A loop listing for Glen Cross rates it difficult, so expect some climbs.

Hockley Valley Provincial Nature Reserve: Ontario Parks describes forested moraines, open meadows and a picturesque gorge cut by the Nottawasaga River. There are no visitor facilities, so bring water.
Cam Snell Side Trail: named for a Ministry of Natural Resources superintendent who helped the club build trails on provincial land in the late 1980s. We didn't find a description of its terrain.
Dogs: allowed on leash throughout. Detailed terrain notes for these trails were not found, so allow extra time.

subtitle: Mono Centre & Mono Cliffs Provincial Park
expect: Parking: the gravel lot at the Mono Community Centre, about 200 m south of Mono Centre on County Road 8. The park's own lot on 3rd Line is pay parking; you won't need it today.

Main Bruce Trail through Mono Cliffs Provincial Park: about 6 km of the Trail runs through the park, among rocky escarpment cliffs, cedars and ferns. Mostly gentle, with a few steep pitches. The park asks hikers to stay on trails; climbing and scrambling are not allowed.

South Outlier Loop Trail: the park's yellow-marked trail, which the Bruce Trail shares in part. It's named for one of the park's two large outliers, chunks of escarpment separated from the main cliff edge.
Road walking: short stretches of the main Trail and the Whitetail Refuge Side Trail follow road shoulders. Keep the dog close.
Whitetail Refuge, Springwater and Laidlaw side trails: no published descriptions were found. The short Hockley Heights spur (0.2 km) is an out-and-back.
Dogs: allowed on leash in the park. Check yourself and the dog for ticks afterwards.

subtitle: Mono Centre and Mono Cliffs Provincial Park
expect: Parking: Gravel lot at the Mono Community Centre, just south of Mono Centre on County Road 8. This is outside the provincial park's pay lot.
Laidlaw Side Trail: Links Mono Centre with the Bruce Trail and includes a stretch on the road shoulder. Keep Zappy close there. No other description of this trail was found.

South Outlier Loop: Starts with a climb up the hill, then levels off on top. The western side follows the cliff edge and has an unofficial lookout facing the cliffs. Stay back from the edge with the dog.
Carriage and Walter Tovell trails: Park trails through shady forest and across an open meadow. The Walter Tovell is a wide, flat path. Expect wooden staircases on the Carriage Trail.
McCarston's Lake Side Trail: A short spur toward McCarston's Lake, a kettle lake left by melting glacial ice.
Main Trail and Springwater Side Trail: One main-trail stretch follows a road shoulder, so keep the leash short there. No details were found for the short Springwater Side Trail.
Bugs: Visitor guides advise bug spray and tick checks. Ontario Parks notes that park trails are not maintained in winter.

subtitle: Mono Cliffs Provincial Park
expect: Parking: There is only limited roadside parking on the south side of 25 Sideroad at the Walter Tovell Side Trail, and you must not block the gate. If it is full, use the larger lot up the road on 2nd Line EHS. Visitor guides warn that parking elsewhere on roads around the park can get you fined or towed.
Walter Tovell Side Trail: A wide, flat path, the longest trail in the park and the bulk of this hike.
Carriage Side Trail: Mostly shady forest plus one large meadow. A large wooden staircase drops into the forest, and another staircase near the viewing platform leads down to the rock formations.
South Outlier Loop: Begins with a climb, then runs fairly flat on top. The western side follows the cliff edge, with a lookout facing the cliffs. Keep Zappy close along the edge.
Lookout Side Trail: A short spur to a lookout over the hardwood forest below.
Season and bugs: Expect crowds at peak times. Bring bug spray and check for ticks. Ontario Parks notes that trails are not maintained in winter.

New side-trail network: On September 25, 2026 the trails here were reconfigured because of seasonal flooding: a damaged bridge was removed and a low-lying section was rerouted. The former Boyne Valley Side Trail is now main Trail, and the Meadows, Centre Road, Murphy's Pinnacle and Boyne Valley Rim side trails are new. Older maps and signs may not match.
Murphy's Pinnacle Side Trail: A 660 m side trail to a scenic viewpoint, early in the route.
Boyne Valley Rim and Meadows side trails: The 2.5 km Rim trail is the spine of this loop, and the 1.2 km Meadows trail closes it. No published descriptions of their terrain were found yet.

Primrose Loop and Prince of Wales side trails: Unchanged by the 2026 work. The Primrose Loop is about 4 km across the Primrose area; Prince of Wales is a short connector. No terrain details were found.
Wayfinding: There is no posted trail map in the park, so follow the blue side-trail blazes and the guide's directions.

Pine River valley: A 2015 trip report describes the main trail following the riverbank through the Pine River Provincial Fishing Area. It passes the concrete shell of an old Dufferin Light and Power generating station and runs along the banks of a fishing pond.
Bell Lookout Side Trail: A very short spur to a lookout, a good place for a snack. Nearby the main trail passes through mixed forest and climbs to another lookout.
Kilgorie, Carl Alexander, Melodonna and Pine River Valley side trails: No descriptions of these side trails were found. Expect the climbs and descents of the river valley.

expect: Parking: Bruce Trail lot on the north side of County Rd 91, 850 m west of Concession 10. Not accessible in winter.

Walker Aggregates Side Trail: The link between the lot and the other trails on this route. A local news story says the blue sign for the kiln side trail is about 400 m from the lot. No other description was found.

Franks Lime Kiln: A restored lime kiln from the mid-1800s, said to be one of the best preserved in Ontario. It sits on private land opened to the public through the Bruce Trail. Part of the side trail goes down a steep slope, so wear good footwear; stay on the paths and behind the safety barriers.

Field & Forest Side Trail: A 720 m side trail opened in August 2025 by the Blue Mountains club with the Escarpment Biosphere Conservancy. It winds through EBC land and makes a short loop with the main Trail on the BTC's Lime Kiln Bluffs Nature Reserve and part of the Walker Aggregates Side Trail.
Short outing: At about 3.2 km this is a short walk; no terrain details for the main Trail stretch were found.

expect: Parking: A small NVCA lot at 8861 Nottawasaga 15/16 Sideroad, open dawn to dusk. A day pass costs $15 + HST per vehicle; buy it through HotSpot or scan the QR code on site. Approach through Singhampton, as the NVCA directs. It warns that map apps may route you along 15/16 Sideroad and Concession 8, which it advises against.
Keyhole Side Trail: Takes you through narrow crevices in the rock, which the NVCA calls an "other-worldly experience." Snow can linger in the crevices into June. Expect tight spots with the dog.
Nottawasaga Bluffs Lookout Side Trail: Leads toward views over the surrounding countryside. The NVCA lists its lookout trail as open only part of the year.
Main Bruce Trail: One loop description notes an old limestone kiln along this stretch.
Caution: The area is a natural hazard area with fissures, crevices and cliffs that can be hidden. Stay on the marked trail. Dogs must be leashed.

expect: Parking: A designated lot 380 m north of the trail crossing on Pretty River Rd. Parking on the road itself is not allowed. The park is non-operating with no washrooms.
Pretty River Access Side Trail: Climbs right away, through a cedar thicket with tightly packed trunks.

Pretty River Side Trail: Passes Sundown Lake, then tops out and descends with some good views. Lower down, a river has several small waterfalls and a few short boardwalks. Near the end there is a spot to wade, which hikers say dogs enjoy.
Main Bruce Trail: Hilly, with steep grades in places. Parts were damaged in a windstorm, so expect fallen trees. The town's trail map marks the highest point on the Bruce Trail (540 m) nearby.
Russ McConnell Side Trail: A loop of under 1 km off the main trail. No details of its terrain were found.
Plants: Watch for poison ivy and giant hogweed, which can cause severe burns. The town asks that pets stay leashed.

Len Gertler Side Trail: Blue-blazed, through the Len Gertler Memorial Loree Forest, named for an environmentalist who helped shape the Niagara Escarpment Plan. A trip report calls it well maintained and well marked, mostly level with exposed roots and rocks.
Views: A clearing and wooden platform at the north end of the forest normally give views of Georgian Bay.
Short outing: At about 2.7 km this is an easy half-day, all on side trails.

John Haigh Side Trail: Follows the 2nd Line road allowance and passes the highest point on the entire Bruce Trail. Parts run on the road shoulder, so keep the dog close.
Petun Side Trail: The longest leg of the hike. It includes a road-shoulder stretch, where the dog should stay close. No further description was found.
Black Ash Creek Side Trail: A short access trail from the parking area. No details were found.

Intercept Side Trail: A short (about 200 m) blue-blazed link between a road curve and the main Bruce Trail.
Swiss Meadows Side Trail: We found no published description of this side trail; expect a mix of trail and road-shoulder walking per the route.

Road walking: The route begins and ends on a road section of the main Bruce Trail. Walk on the shoulder and keep Zappy close.

Main Bruce Trail: White-blazed. A trail guide describes it dropping through a steep valley and climbing to a ridge with views north, then running west near the top of the private Georgian Peaks ski club.

Len Gertler Memorial Loree Forest: The Len Gertler Side Trail (blue blazes) loops through this forest, named for an environmentalist who helped shape the Niagara Escarpment Plan. Length: At about 12.3 km this is a full day; most of it is on the main trail getting to and from the Len Gertler loop.

expect: Parking: Roadside on the east side of Townline Road, north of the entrance to the Townline Access Side Trail.
Metcalfe Rock: The main trail climbs the side of Metcalfe Rock; one trip report describes a fine view from the summit across the Mill Creek Valley.

Crevices and caves: Large dolostone slabs have broken away to form crevices and caves; the short Metcalfe Crevice Side Trail descends through a rocky gorge about 30 m high. It is described as very challenging, more so with ice or snow. Crevices have long drops and off-trail chutes are easy to get lost in; keep Zappy on a short leash.
Chuck & Pat Grant Side Trail: A magazine walk describes the side trail descending the north side of Metcalfe Rock, with the forest changing from deciduous to coniferous.
Townline Access Side Trail: Links the roadside parking to the main trail; no further details were found.

Old Baldy lookout: A series of rocky outlooks over the Beaver Valley and Kimberley. Footing is uneven with exposed rock and roots, and can be icy in winter.

Cliff edges: The lookouts are on an unprotected edge of the Niagara Escarpment with steep drop-offs. Keep Zappy on a short leash and well back from the edge. Rock climbing is permitted here, so you may meet climbers.

subtitle: Eagle's Summit Nature Reserve, Beaver Valley
expect: Parking: Beaver Valley Lookout on the west side of Grey Rd 13, roughly 750 m north of the Bruce Trail. The Beaver Valley club notes parking and washrooms close to the new trail network.

Eagle's Summit Nature Reserve: About 123 acres of escarpment forest, meadows, karst, and hawthorn and apple groves just south of Kimberley, named for the Bald Eagles seen overhead. Listen for Ovenbird, American Redstart and Black-and-white Warbler.
Main Trail: Rerouted in July 2025 along the escarpment crest; the 2.4 km reroute moved about 1.6 km of trail off roads and into forest and meadow with panoramic views.

New side trails: Seven side trails opened in 2025, including the 3.2 km East Mountain loop and the short Cascades, Valley Vistas, Rockface, East Eagle's Summit, Pond View and Erratic View trails. Together they reach forests, meadows, rock faces, gorges, ponds and wide views of the Beaver Valley. Individual trail descriptions were not published.
Valley Crossover Side Trail: No published description was found.
Cautions: With rock faces and gorges on this network, keep Zappy close and stay back from edges. At 11.1 km with many junctions, follow the guide's directions closely.

expect: Parking: Limited roadside parking on the south side of East Back Line.

Boyne River & main trail: Forested trail that follows the Boyne River, crosses it, and runs up and down along the escarpment. A local club describes packed trail with lots of roots and many small-to-medium hills, plus one longer climb (easy to moderate). Poles are recommended.
Bridges and boardwalks: Expect several bridges and many boardwalks, built in 2023 by Beaver Valley Bruce Trail volunteers. Boardwalks can be slippery when wet.

Ferns and views: Look for maidenhair and hart's-tongue ferns. A trip report describes rugged terrain above the Boyne River with cascading waterfalls and a high meadow with views across to Cuckoo Valley and north down the Beaver Valley.
Upper Beaver Valley Side Trail: Includes a road-shoulder section; keep Zappy close there. The Uplands Meadow Side Trail is part of the club's loop here.

subtitle: Kimberley Forest & Wodehouse Karst
expect: Parking: Roadside on 7th Line at the start of the Wodehouse Karst Side Trail.

Wodehouse Karst: Described as having one of the finest groups of sinkholes in southern Ontario. Wodehouse Creek disappears into a sinkhole and later re-emerges as a small cascade down the valley slope. There are views toward Old Baldy. Stay on the trail: the area mixes private and public land.

Kimberley Forest: About 1,000 acres, mostly Crown land, with the Bruce Trail running north–south through it and the Beaver River flowing across the base of the forest. Licensed hunting and trapping are permitted, so in fall wear bright colours and put a bright vest on Zappy.
Road walking: The Kimberley Forest and Valley Crossover side trails each include road-shoulder stretches. Keep Zappy close.
Valley Crossover Side Trail: We found no published description of this side trail beyond the route data.
Length: At about 12.8 km this is one of the longer days; allow extra time.

subtitle: Silent Valley Nature Reserve
expect: Parking: Limited roadside parking at the north end of 2nd Concession S, off Grey Rd 18 near Bognor. The Silent Valley Side Trail leads in from there.

Silent Valley: A 200-acre Bruce Trail Conservancy reserve with wetland, reforested farmland, old cedar and hardwood forest, and a stretch of the Niagara Escarpment. The club rates its loop moderate to strenuous, with steep, rocky escarpment sections and large tumbled dolostone.

Main Trail & Avalanche Pass: The Main Trail runs along the top of the escarpment. The Avalanche side trail explores the talus slope below it. Both are described as the more challenging trails here, so expect rocky, uneven footing.
Vanishing Wall Side Trail: A short spur. We found no published description of it.

Wilson Homestead Side Trail: The easy part of the walk. It passes the stone foundation of a settler's barn with fossils in its walls, a stone-lined well about 20 ft deep and the wreckage of a Cessna that crashed in a 1970 storm, now a memorial with a plaque. Keep Zappy well back from the open well.

subtitle: Woodford & Crevice Springs
expect: Parking: Along Woodford Crescent, plus a large lot at the Woodford Community Hall.
Road walking: The Main Trail follows the road shoulder in two places, including along Woodford Crescent and a laneway out of the hamlet. Keep Zappy close.

Main Trail through Woodford: The trail passes a glacial pothole once used as a pioneer lime kiln, a stream that disappears and comes back as a waterfall (best in spring) and the ruins of a pioneer cabin and barn. The trail is rocky, and you may have to cross streams in spring.

Crevices: The club's loop climbs the escarpment through two narrow crevices that can stay icy into late spring. One writer called a crevice here “a tight squeeze”. The club mentions a bypass side trail around them, which may be easier with a dog.

Crevice Springs: A 47-acre Bruce Trail Conservancy property with a bridge over a crevice, caves and crevices that stay cool even in a heat wave, and seven springs flowing from the talus slope. The trail climbs back up the talus to the top of the escarpment. In spring, listen for black-throated blue warblers.
Woodford Escarpment Side Trail: The club's loop uses it to get back to the Main Trail. We found no further description of it.

subtitle: Bayview Escarpment Provincial Nature Reserve
expect: Parking: Roadside along the St. Vincent-Sydenham Townline at the field entrance to the River Kwai Side Trail. The reserve has no visitor facilities, so bring water and plan for the full 12 km.
River Kwai Side Trail: Hikers describe crossing an old logging road, walking about 1.5 km through hardwood forest, then crossing a field and the River Kwai Bridge.

Bayview Escarpment: A dolostone-capped promontory with nearly 8 km of sensitive slopes and cliffs, crevice caves, exposed bedrock, fern colonies including rare species, and a swamp at the base. Ontario Parks asks visitors to tread lightly.

Main Trail along the edge: About 2.5 km follows the scarp edge through cedar and hardwood, with broad views over the Meaford Tank Range to Georgian Bay and Collingwood. The footing is broken dolostone cobbles and old cart tracks, and one writer called parts of the cliff edge “perilous”. Keep Zappy close.
Military neighbour: The reserve borders the Meaford Land Forces Training Centre. Fences carry “No Trespassing” signs, and you may hear or see tank manoeuvres. Stay on the trail.
Kaboom & Bayview Escarpment side trails: Short spurs off the Main Trail. We found no published description of either.
Road walking: The last part of the route follows a road shoulder on the Main Trail and then the River Kwai Side Trail (trip reports place this on the St. Vincent-Sydenham Townline). Keep Zappy close.

Pines Side Trail: A loop through a white pine plantation and an old apple orchard, past the remains of a pioneer cabin and the stonework of a settler's barn.
Clearview Side Trail: Follows a wetland with marsh marigolds in early spring, and it can be muddy. In spring, salmon spawn in a tributary of Bothwell Creek.

subtitle: Harrison Park & the Palisades, Owen Sound
expect: Parking: Free parking in several places in Harrison Park. The park also has a year-round restaurant (Harrison Park Inn) and a campground.

Harrison Park Side Trail: Easy walking on wide, hard-packed paths through hardwood forest and parkland along the Sydenham River. It passes the Black History Cairn and a boardwalk view of Weaver's Creek falls. The falls are on private land, so view them from the boardwalk.

Palisades Side Trail: Moderate to difficult, with rugged, rocky uphill sections. It climbs the lower talus of the escarpment through a canyon with cliffs on both sides and fern glens, past the Devil's Playhouse, a rock overhang behind an easy-to-miss, unmarked narrow opening in the cliff.
Raven's Nest: A very short side trail up to a lookout at the top of the escarpment. Keep Zappy close near the edge.
Creamery Hill Side Trail: Includes two road-shoulder stretches. Keep Zappy close on the road. We found little published detail on its terrain.

subtitle: Jones Falls & Memorial Forest, west of Owen Sound
expect: Parking: Park at the Grey-Bruce Tourist Information Office. You enter from Hwy 6, just north of the junction of Hwys 6 and 21. Ontario Nature Trails lists no fee.

Merle Gunby Side Trail: A blue-blazed trail on natural and rocky ground, rated moderate, through hardwood forest. It links the tourist office lot to the main Bruce Trail, and a short spur leads south to Jones Falls.

Jones Falls: Owen Sound Tourism says the Pottawatomi River drops about 12 m over the Escarpment here and recommends the bridge for the best view. From the top you can stand at the lip of the falls and look straight down, so keep Zappy well back from the edge. Trilliums line the trail in spring.
Memorial Forest Side Trail: The Sydenham club suggests taking this side trail down to the base of Jones Falls for a close-up view. Expect a descent, then a climb back up to the main trail.

Dogs: Zappy stays on leash. The Sydenham club asks that dogs be leashed and kept under control, especially near farmland, and suggests an orange or fluorescent harness or bandana in hunting season so a dog isn't mistaken for wildlife.

expect: Parking: Free parking in several places in Harrison Park. One option is to drive east past the restaurant, cross the bridge and turn left right away into a parking area. Owen Sound Tourism confirms that entry and parking are free.

Harrison Park: More than 40 hectares of streams, gardens and forest along the Sydenham River, with wide, hard-packed trails. Weavers' Creek Falls can be seen from a boardwalk. The park's trails connect directly with the Bruce Trail toward Inglis Falls. The Harrison Park Inn restaurant is open year-round.

Keeling Side Trail: Blue-blazed, natural-surface trail rated moderate. Ontario Nature Trails describes it starting near the Inglis Falls parking area, so you may pass close to the falls. It runs east to Highways 6 & 10, which you cross before a short jog south.
Road walking: Two stretches of the Keeling Side Trail follow a road shoulder, and one includes the crossing of Highways 6 & 10. Keep Zappy close and on a short leash, and cross carefully.

Sydenham Nature Reserve Side Trail: The Keeling trail meets the Owen Sound rail trail and joins the Sydenham Nature Reserve Side Trail, a loop through the reserve before you return the way you came. We didn't find detailed terrain notes for the reserve loop.
Length: At 12.5 km this is one of the longer outings, so plan for a full morning or afternoon. Picnic areas and washrooms are listed at the Inglis Falls trailhead.

subtitle: The Glen & East Linton escarpment, north of Owen Sound
expect: Parking: Roadside parking at the base of the Escarpment on East Linton Rd, at the East Linton Access Trail. Ontario Nature Trails calls the parking limited. There is no fee.

The Glen: The Sydenham club describes the Glen as a horseshoe-shaped indentation in the Escarpment carved by glaciers. Its cliff tops overlook a wetland that draws waterfowl. From the top, Ontario Nature Trails says the view is "like looking onto a bay of tree tops."

Frank Holley Side Trail: Rated difficult, with natural and rocky footing. It descends the Escarpment and passes through a series of crevices. Watch for fossils on a rock overhang and a lookout. Take the crevices slowly with Zappy on a short leash, since footing and spacing can be awkward for a dog.
Walker Homestead Side Trail: A very short spur off the Frank Holley Side Trail. We didn't find a published description of it.
Main Bruce Trail: The white-blazed main trail links these side trails along the Escarpment.

expect: Parking: There is room for several cars on Kemble Rock Rd at the Nels Maher Side Trail.

Kemble Mountain: A trip report describes the main trail after Kemble Rock Rd running along a wide dolostone outcrop on top of the Escarpment, then through shady forest with dense Canadian wild ginger, ferns and mushrooms. It's a good choice for a hot day.

Dodd's Hill: The Sydenham club says the stretch from Kemble Mountain to Dodd's Hill is "filled with fissures" and full of ferns. Watch your footing and keep Zappy on a short leash near the cracks in the rock.

Edmonstone and Nels Maher side trails: Together with the main trail they form a loop of about 3 km through mixed hardwood forest, according to Ontario Nature Trails. The short Dodds Hill Side Trail is a quick spur off the main trail.

Dogs: Zappy stays on leash. The Sydenham club asks that dogs be leashed and kept under control, especially near farmland, and suggests an orange or fluorescent harness or bandana in hunting season so a dog isn't mistaken for wildlife.

expect: Parking: Enter the parking area from Grey Rd 1, about 4.8 km east of Wiarton. Grey Sauble Conservation charges a parking fee in spring, summer and fall; pay online through the GSCA site, or use a GSCA parking membership. The laneway is not maintained in winter.
Trail to Caves: The GSCA trail leads from the parking area to the caves on a moderate path of compacted soil, packed earth and stone. It is not wheelchair accessible.
The caves: Sea caves along the escarpment face, carved by the waves of post-glacial Lake Algonquin thousands of years ago. You can also read about Robert Bruce, who once lived on the property.

Colpoy's Cavern Side Trail: A short Bruce Trail side trail that branches off the caves trail. Specific details on its terrain were not found; expect escarpment rock and forest footing, and take care near the cave openings.

subtitle: Kemble Rock & Kemble Wetland (BTC nature reserve)
expect: Parking: Roadside parking on the shoulder of Cole's Side Rd, where it turns into a logging road. Don't block the logging road. In April 2026 the BTC reported Coles Road closed to traffic because of flooding, so in wet seasons check conditions before you drive up.

Kemble trail network: This web of side trails opened in 2019 across 316 acres of Bruce Trail Conservancy land. A BTC club hike rated it moderate, with some hills, poor footing and muddy sections, crevices, and mature cedar and hardwood forest. A guidebook rates the loops moderate to strenuous.

Cliff edge and crevices: Part of the main Bruce Trail here follows a narrow ledge along the cliff face, and a guidebook warns that many crevices lie above the cliff edge. Keep Zappy on a short leash and close to you.
Cedar Point Side Trail: A short loop to a lookout over a marsh and an area of shallow open water.

Kemble Wetland Side Trail: It leads to a clearing at the edge of a large wetland, through meadow, hawthorn thicket and mature hardwood forest. Watch for a big fallen tree with a hole cut through it. Club hikers skip this trail when it's too wet.
Mystery Cabin and Coles side trails: The Mystery Cabin route passes the ruins of a small cabin overlooking a view. We didn't find descriptions of the MapleCross Ridge or Birch Camp side trails.
Length: At 12.5 km this is a long day. The many short loops add up, so bring water and snacks for you and Zappy.

subtitle: Slough of Despond, Georgian Bluffs
expect: Parking: Roadside parking on Colpoy's Range Rd. Don't park in the gateway or on the loading ramp. A BTC hike listing calls trailhead parking limited. In 2020, a trip report found the eastern part of Colpoy's Range Rd partly flooded and impassable for ordinary cars, so come from the west if it's wet.

Slough of Despond Side Trail: An out-and-back on one long side trail, about 11.4 km in total. A BTC hike listing describes the area as relatively flat through fields and forest, with some crevices and "magnificent views of the bay and Slough of Despond."
Stiles: That BTC loop hike also mentions three stiles with no way around. If you meet stiles, be ready to help Zappy over.

The Slough: A cattail-fringed wetland that a trip report says was left behind when glacial Lake Algonquin was cut off about 11,000 years ago. From Cole's Sideroad you can look west across it to Esther's Bluff.

Flooding: In April 2026 the BTC closed the main trail between Big Bay Sideroad and the Colpoy's Range Rd parking because of flooding, then reopened it on April 29. Expect wet ground in spring and after heavy rain.

subtitle: Skinner's Bluff & Colpoy's Bay
expect: Parking: Roadside parking on Gleason Lake Rd, where the Curly Harnden and Len Holley side trails meet (near the Colpoy's Range Rd corner).
Len Holley Side Trail: A blue-blazed trail heading north about 1.8 km from Gleason Lake Rd to the main Bruce Trail. You walk it both ways.

Skinner's Bluff on the main trail: The main trail follows the top of the Escarpment, with views across Colpoy's Bay. blogTO calls it a fairly difficult hike along the cliff's edge, climbing steadily to several lookouts. From the top you can see White Cloud, Griffith and Hay islands. Keep Zappy on a short leash at the lookouts.
Skinner's Woods and Chris Walker side trails: The Chris Walker Side Trail is a 1.3 km blue-blazed loop off the main trail. We didn't find a description of the Skinner's Woods Side Trail.
Length: At 12.6 km this is a long day. The Sydenham club notes many good picnic spots along the Skinner's Bluff stretch.

Dogs: Zappy stays on leash. The Sydenham club asks that dogs be leashed and kept under control, especially near farmland, and suggests an orange or fluorescent harness or bandana in hunting season so a dog isn't mistaken for wildlife.

Main Bruce Trail along the bluffs: The Sydenham club describes the 11 km from Skinner's Bluff to Bruce's Caves as having many lookouts over Colpoy's Bay and plenty of picnic spots. Ontario Nature Trails notes views north over the bay to the Malcolm Bluffs. Stay back from cliff edges with Zappy.
Bruce's Caves: These caves were formed by wave action from post-glacial Lake Algonquin. The conservation area's trail is rated moderate, with compacted-soil and stone surfaces.

Dogs: Zappy stays on leash. The Sydenham club asks that dogs be leashed and kept under control, especially near farmland, and suggests an orange or fluorescent harness or bandana in hunting season so a dog isn't mistaken for wildlife.

Gravelly Point Side Trail: Ontario Nature describes a 4 km side-trail loop from the Mallory Beach Road parking. It follows an old logging road, drops to the Georgian Bay shoreline, and returns to the lot. This appears to be the Gravelly Point Side Trail.
Shoreline and climb: The reserve has about 4 km of undeveloped shingle beach on Colpoys Bay. It rises more than 110 m from the beach to the top of the escarpment, so expect a real descent and climb.
Wildlife: Malcolm Bluff Shores is a large, unbroken forest. Black bears and peregrine falcons have been seen here, along with several rare ferns. Keep Zappy close.

The trail also passes the site of the Legend of Spirit Rock. Paths through Spirit Rock Conservation Area cross fields and forest, and an escarpment-top lookout gives wide views over Colpoy's Bay.

Spiral staircase: A spiral staircase on the Bruce Trail winds down the cliff between the escarpment top and the rocky Colpoy's Bay shore. Take it slowly with Zappy, and stay back from the cliff edge at the lookout.
Wiarton Side Trail: A short connector back toward town. We found no description of it.
Season: Spirit Rock Conservation Area is open year-round, but its trails aren't groomed in winter.

Footing: Expect uneven ground through the boulder area, and possible wet spots near the beaver ponds. Allow extra time for a 4 km loop.

Colpoy's Bluff Side Trail: The longest stretch of the day. Ontario Nature Trails describes about 4 km of blue blazes between the Crawford Dr Side Trail and the Whicher Side Trail. We found no description of its footing.
Whicher Side Trail and the disappearing stream: A short spur off the Whicher Side Trail leads to a disappearing stream, which a Hike Bike Travel writer counted among the trail's "gems".

Main Bruce Trail along Colpoy's Bay Bluff: A 2015 trip report describes mature forest along the escarpment edge with little elevation change and firm, sometimes rocky footing. It mentions occasional spectacular lookouts over Colpoy's Bay. Sharon's Bench, a memorial to Bruce Trail hiker Sharon France, sits near the Mallory Beach Side Trail.
Cliff edge: The same report notes large dolostone blocks along the edge that looked ready to fall. Stay back from the lip at lookouts and keep Zappy close on a short leash.
Distance: At 12.6 km, this is a full day. Bring enough water for both of you, since the route has no amenities.

Gatis and Mallory Beach Side Trails: Short blue-blazed connectors. Ontario Nature Trails uses them as shortcuts in the Colpoy's Bluff loop, but it doesn't describe them. We found no details on their footing.

Main Bruce Trail along Malcolm Bluff: A 2015 trip report describes the escarpment edge as mature forest with little elevation change and firm, sometimes rocky footing. It mentions good views of Hay, Griffith and White Cloud Islands at the mouth of Colpoy's Bay. Stay back from the edge, where the report noted loose dolostone blocks.

Bob Light and Malcolm Bluff Side Trails: Just before the Malcolm Bluff turn, the trail crosses an alvar, a stretch of open dolostone pavement with little soil. Ontario Nature Trails rates the area loop moderate, on natural and rocky ground.
Wildlife: This area borders Malcolm Bluff Shores Nature Reserve, where black bears have been recorded.
Distance: At 12.9 km, this is a long day. Ontario Nature Trails rates the Coveney's Side Trail area difficult, so pace yourselves and carry plenty of water.

Climbing Sydney Bay Bluff: A 2015 trip report describes the main trail climbing a forested talus slope near Boundary Bluffs, with a steel staircase up the final cliff. From the top, Hope Bay lies below.

Lookouts: The route makes several short trips out to viewpoints. A paddling guide calls the Bruce Trail lookout at Sydney Bluff "spectacular". These are open cliff edges, so keep Zappy on a short leash.
Boundary Bluffs and Hart's Tongue Side Trails: These two blue-blazed trails make up most of the day. We found no detailed descriptions of their footing.
Distance: At 12.2 km with a big climb, this is a demanding day. Bring plenty of water.

Jack Poste Side Trail: This side trail leads to glacial potholes worn into the bedrock. Trilliums bloom along it in May. The Hope Bay Lookout nearby gives panoramic views of the bay from the escarpment top.

Main Bruce Trail: Follows the escarpment edge. A 2015 trip report describes this stretch as rugged edge paths with spectacular lookouts and glacial potholes. A signed deep crevice lies along the edge, so keep Zappy close.
Wildlife: A 2020 hiker reported a black bear near the signed crevice. The bear moved off.

Hopeness Side Trail and road walking: The Hopeness Side Trail leads out to Richardson Rd. From there, the Jack Poste Side Trail follows roads, including Hopeness Rd and Cathedral Dr, back to the car. Walk the shoulder with Zappy close.

subtitle: Barrow Bay
expect: Parking: Use the Bruce Trail lot off Bruce Rd 9 in Barrow Bay. The local club asks hikers not to park on the west side of Bruce Rd 9.

Barrow Bay Cliffs: The main trail south of Barrow Bay runs through the Bruce Trail Conservancy's Barrow Bay Cliffs Nature Reserve (bought in 2019), a newer section that passes cliffs, lookouts and dense forest, with a staircase from the escarpment edge down to the shoreline. Keep Zappy close near the cliff edges.

John Appleton & Beth Gilhespy Side Trails: The John Appleton loop passes a beaver pond and winds through hardwood forest and fractured dolostone rock on a natural, moderate surface. Watch your footing (and paws) on the cracked rock.
Medicine Path & Hawthorn Side Trails: Short connectors (0.7 km and 0.1 km). No specific trail descriptions were found.
Road walking: Parts of the main trail follow the shoulder of Bruce Rd 9 near Barrow Bay, at the start and end of the day. Keep Zappy on a short leash and on the outside, away from traffic.

subtitle: Lion's Head Provincial Nature Reserve
expect: Parking: The lot outside the reserve gate (via Evergreen Rd or Cemetery Rd) has only a few spots, so arrive early.

Cemetery Road & Ilse Hanel Side Trails: These lead from the parking to the main trail. The Ilse Hanel Side Trail is blue-blazed and is part of the reserve's perimeter loop. No detailed terrain descriptions were found.

Main Bruce Trail (escarpment edge): The main trail around the reserve often runs very close to the cliff edge. Expect technical rock, glacial potholes on the clifftop, ancient white cedars and big Georgian Bay lookouts. Keep Zappy close at the edge and go when it's dry if you can.
Inland Side Trail: A 2.3 km stretch through the interior of the reserve, away from the cliffs. Inland, the reserve is known for wildflower-rich woodland and karst landforms.
Facilities: There are no visitor facilities in the reserve, so bring water for you and Zappy.

Inland & Geodetic Side Trails: Short blue-blazed trails into the reserve's interior, which has wildflower-rich woodland and karst landforms. The Geodetic spur is only 0.1 km long. No other details were found.

expect: Parking: Roadside on the shoulders of Cape Chin North Rd. Pull fully off the road.
Otter Lake Side Trail: A 2.2 km blue-blazed trail. No specific description was found.

Main Bruce Trail & Bard Side Trail: Around Cape Chin the main trail passes a beaver pond and crosses several old pastures. The short Bard Side Trail (about 0.5 km) is a cut-across between the trails near Cape Chin.
Cape Chin Meadows Side Trail: Winds through old farm fields, bush lots and back roads. A club group hiking here saw signs of black bears, so keep Zappy leashed and close.

subtitle: Cape Chin
expect: Parking: Roadside on the eastern shoulder of Cape Chin North Rd, where the side trail enters. Pull fully off the road.

Cape Chin Meadows Side Trail: Part of the club's Friendship Trail loop near Cape Chin. It winds through old farm fields, bush lots and back roads. A club group hiking here found signs of black bears (overturned rocks, apple feeding), so keep Zappy leashed and close.
Main Bruce Trail: The main trail here has cliff-edge views of Georgian Bay with rocky climbs and descents. Keep Zappy close near the edge.
Pat Daunt Side Trail: A short 0.6 km spur. No specific description was found.
Road walking: The final stretch of the Cape Chin Meadows Side Trail follows a road shoulder back toward the car. Keep Zappy close.

route: Cottrill Lake Side Trail > Anne & Clayton Roberts Side Trail > Main Trail > Lillie Family Side Trail > Lillie Pothole Side Trail > Lillie Family Side Trail > Minhinnick Side Trail > Devil's Monument Side Trail > Main Trail > Lillie Family Side Trail
subtitle: Devil's Monument
expect: Parking: Bruce Trail parking with direct access to the Cottrill Lake, Anne & Clayton Roberts and Lillie Family Side Trails.

Devil's Monument: A flowerpot (a rock pillar shaped by erosion), described as the only complete flowerpot on land along the east side of the peninsula. A short side trail leads to a series of steps down the escarpment to its base. Take the stairs slowly with Zappy.
Main Bruce Trail: Hikers report a spectacular escarpment-edge view north over Dyers Bay. Keep Zappy close at the edge.

Cottrill Lake, Anne & Clayton Roberts, Lillie Family & Minhinnick Side Trails: Side trails on lands owned by the Ontario Heritage Trust and managed by the Bruce Trail Conservancy. No specific terrain descriptions were found. The Lillie Pothole spur is only 0.1 km.
Road walking: Parts of the main trail and of the Minhinnick and Lillie Family Side Trails follow road shoulders. Keep Zappy close.

subtitle: Little Cove
expect: Parking: Use the small off-road lot only. Roadside parking is prohibited and enforced.

Fairway Meadows Side Trail: Added in October 2024 at the invitation of private landowners near Little Cove. It joins the main trail at the Dolostone Arch Nature Reserve and at Little Cove Provincial Nature Reserve, making a loop of about 6 km. Stay on the trail across private land and keep Zappy leashed.
Road walking: Parts of the main trail and the Fairway Meadows Side Trail follow road shoulders. Keep Zappy close.
Terrain: No source described this trail's terrain. Expect typical northern Peninsula conditions with rocky footing.

subtitle: Fathom Five National Marine Park, Tobermory
expect: Parking: Use the official municipal lot at the end of Dunks Bay Rd. Northern Bruce Peninsula runs paid parking in Tobermory from May 15 to September 15, and Parks Canada passes are not valid in municipal lots, so check the rules for this lot before you go.

Burnt Point Loop Side Trail: Starts across from the Dunks Bay Lookout and passes through cedar forest and small ponds, with rough, rocky sections (sturdy footwear recommended). There are Georgian Bay views at the halfway point near the tip of Burnt Point. Sections are sometimes closed by high water, so check conditions.
Viewpoint & access trail: A short spur leads to a viewpoint over the bay. Burnt Point is a busy area in summer.
Dogs: 10Adventures notes pets are allowed on leash on the Burnt Point Loop.
Park pass: 10Adventures says a valid Parks Canada pass is required for the Burnt Point Loop. Check before you go.
